extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in Pakistan's blasphemy laws and human rights implications
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain the statutory offences, constitutional context, judicial and enforcement practices, and documented misuse/vigilantism related to Pakistan's blasphemy laws. Focuses on the Pakistan Penal Code sections and how they are applied and abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: §298 — Uttering words/gestures with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who, with the purposeful intent to offend the religious sentiments of another individual, either speaks a word or makes a noise within earshot of that person, or performs a gesture or displays an object within their line of sight, is liable to be penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment: 1–3 years imprisonment, or Rs 500,000 fine, or both. This provision requires purposeful intent to offend (see mens rea entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: §298A — Use of derogatory remarks in respect of holy personages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of derogatory remarks etc., in respect of holy personages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced 1980. Punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment, or fine, or both. Part of the statutory scheme protecting religious figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: §298B — Ahmadi-specific restriction (misuse of epithets etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Ahmadi blasphemy law) Misuse of epithets, descriptions and titles etc., reserved for certain holy personages or places, by Ahmadis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserted 26 April 1984. Punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine. Targets conduct by members of the Ahmadi community and is part of the legal differentiation of Ahmadis.

rubrics_metrics.name: §298C — Ahmadi representation and proselytising prohibition (Ordinance XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Ahmadi blasphemy law) Any Ahmadi representing themself as a Muslim, or preaching or propagating his faith, or 'in any manner whatsoever' outraging the religious feelings of Muslims, or posing himself as a Muslim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserted 26 April 1984. Punishment: Up to 3 years imprisonment and fine. Part of the legal regime that criminalizes Ahmadi religious expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: §295 — Injuring or defiling places of worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Injuring or defiling places of worship, with intent to insult the religion of any class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment: Up to 2 years imprisonment or fine, or both. Requires intent to insult religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: §295A — Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings of any class by insulting its religion or religious beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally enacted 1927. Punishment: Up to 10 years imprisonment, or fine, or both. Requires deliberate and malicious intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: §295B — Defiling the Qur'an
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Added 1982. Punishment: Imprisonment for life. Applied specifically to desecration of the Qur'an.

rubrics_metrics.name: §295C — Derogatory remarks about Prophet Muhammad; mandatory death penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of derogatory remarks, spoken, written, directly or indirectly, etc. defiles the name of Muhammad or other Prophet(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserted 1986 and made (Feb. 1990) a provision carrying a Mandatory Death sentence and fine. The statute provides that trial must take place in a Court of Session with a Muslim judge presiding. Unlike other sections, §295-C has been treated as not requiring the usual intent standard (see mens rea entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mens rea requirement for blasphemy offences (intent requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for §295-C, the provisions of §295 require that an offence be a consequence of the intent of the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most blasphemy provisions require deliberate/malicious intent (e.g., §§295, 295A, §298). This distinction is legally important because §295-C has been applied without the same intent requirement, leading to convictions even in cases where intent is disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional context and state duties (Articles 2, 31, 33, 10A)
rubrics_metrics.description: By its constitution, the official name of Pakistan is the 'Islamic Republic of Pakistan'; Article 2 makes Islam the state religion. Article 31 directs the state to foster the Islamic way of life; Article 33 directs the state to discourage parochial, racial, tribal, sectarian, and provincial prejudices. Article 10A provides for the right to a fair trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constitutional framing is presented as part of why Pakistan has among the strictest anti‑blasphemy laws; it also creates tension between religious protection and guarantees like fair trial rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Shariat Court (FSC) authority and impact on blasphemy law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Shariat Court rules on whether any particular law is repugnant to the injunctions of Islam; if a law is repugnant the President/Governor shall take steps to amend the law so as to bring it into conformity with the Injunctions of Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In October 1990 the FSC ruled that §295-C was repugnant to Islam because it permitted life imprisonment as an alternative to death, and said the penalty for contempt of the Holy Prophet 'is death'. The FSC's rulings can prompt statutory amendments unless overruled by the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPC §153A as a legal countermeasure to misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever 'by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representations or otherwise, promotes or incites... disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups' shall be fined and punished with imprisonment up to five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified in the article as one of the few statutory tools that may be useful to counter misuse of blasphemy laws (e.g., to penalize instigators). Practical effectiveness is limited in the face of social/political pressures described elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement practices and procedural protections (denial of bail, solitary confinement, trial procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those accused of blasphemy are subject to immediate incarceration, and most accused are denied bail to forestall mob violence. It is common for those accused to be put in solitary confinement for their protection. Trials under §295-C must take place in a Court of Session with a Muslim judge presiding (statutory note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences include prolonged pre-trial detention, solitary confinement, and trials without usual evidentiary protections (article notes instances where defense witnesses were not admitted). Those acquitted often go into hiding or leave Pakistan for safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse patterns: extortion, fabricated accusations, and online entrapment
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy laws have been misused to target vulnerable individuals, often through online entrapment, fabricated accusations, or to extort money or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 2023 case where a job seeker was lured to forward an image and arrested; 2024 police report 'Blasphemy Business Group' detailing criminal networks using fabricated accusations. Human rights experts characterize such tactics as used to extort individuals or inflate arrest figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilantism and extrajudicial violence against accused and reformers
rubrics_metrics.description: Those accused of blasphemy (and sometimes police, lawyers, judges, or officials) may be harassed, threatened, attacked, or murdered by mobs or vigilantes. High-profile opponents of the law have been assassinated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article cites numerous examples: assassinations of Salman Taseer and Shahbaz Bhatti, extrajudicial killings of accused (at least 89 killed 1947–2021), mob attacks such as the August 2023 burning of Christian houses in Jaranwala, and killings of persons involved in blasphemy cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet censorship and criminal penalties for online blasphemous content
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has blocked websites (e.g., Facebook in May 2010 over Everybody Draw Muhammad Day) and monitored online platforms; individuals have been convicted and sentenced for sharing blasphemous content on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: May–June 2010 website blocks; January 2021 Anti-Terrorism Court conviction and death sentences for three men who shared blasphemous content on social media; governments have monitored major internet companies for offensive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative development and amendments (historical changes and tightening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy-related laws evolved from colonial-era provisions (1860, 1927) and were expanded and hardened during successive legislatures/governments (e.g., Zia-ul Haq's 1980–1986 'Islamicisation', 1974 Second Amendment declaring Ahmadis non-Muslims, 1982 §295-B, 1986 §295-C). In Jan 2023, the National Assembly passed a bill increasing penalties for disrespecting the Prophet's companions, wives, and family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The timeline demonstrates increasing severity and widening scope of offences; recent parliamentary actions (2023) tightened penalties, raising human-rights concerns among minorities and advocates.
